title: Unknown operators, model mismatch, and robustness limits

items.title: Operator, noise-law, and prior-support mismatch
items.statement:
Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(\mathsf Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty class of admissible truths, and let $q:U	o Q$ assign each truth its recovery target in a metric space $(Q,d_Q)$. Let $\mathfrak A$ index forward maps $F_A:U	o\mathsf Y$; in this definition an **operator** means such a forward map, and linearity is not assumed. A specified set $\mathcal C\subseteq U	imes\mathfrak A$ records which truth/operator pairs are admissible; no full-product assumption is made. Equip $\mathsf Y$ with a sigma-algebra $\mathcal Y$ and an addition operation such that every translation $	au_z(e)=z+e$ is measurable. A **noise law** is a probability measure $
u$ on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$. For each admissible pair $(x,A)\in\mathcal C$, the observation random element on the probability space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y,
u)$ is $e\mapsto F_A(x)+e$, and its sampling law is
$$P_{x,A,
u}(B)=
u igl(\{e\in\mathsf Y:F_A(x)+e\in B\} igr),\qquad B\in\mathcal Y.$$
The translation measurability assumption makes this law a probability measure.

For a true specification $(x_\star,A_\star,
u_\star)$ with $(x_\star,A_\star)\in\mathcal C$ and a specified working operator $\widetilde A$ and noise law $\widetilde
u$, there is **operator mismatch at the truth** when $F_{A_\star}(x_\star)
e F_{\widetilde A}(x_\star)$, and there is **noise-law mismatch** when $
u_\star
e\widetilde
u$. A **working statistical model** is a metric index space $(\Xi,d_\Xi)$, a family $(Q_\xi)_{\xi\in\Xi}$ of sampling laws on the same data space, and a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on a sigma-algebra containing every open metric ball. The statistical model is **misspecified** for true observation law $P_\star=P_{x_\star,A_\star,
u_\star}$ when $P_\star
otin\{Q_\xi:\xi\in\Xi\}$. If a true model index $\xi_\star\in\Xi$ is specified, there is a **prior-support mismatch** at $\xi_\star$ when some open ball $B_\Xi(\xi_\star,r)$, $r>0$, has $\Pi(B_\Xi(\xi_\star,r))=0$. These are distinct properties; an operator or noise-law mismatch need not by itself make the statistical model misspecified or exclude the true index from the prior's support. This definition makes no assertion about posterior existence or convergence.
items.strategy: Specify a measurable additive-noise observation law as the law of a translated noise random element, then distinguish operator, noise-law, sampling-model, and prior-support discrepancies.

items.title: Equal observation laws force a metric-risk lower bound
items.statement:
Let $(Q,d_Q)$ be a metric target space and let $\mathcal G$ be a sigma-algebra on $Q$. Let $\tau_i=(x_i,A_i,\nu_i)$, $i\in\{0,1\}$, be two admissible truth/operator/noise specifications on one measurable data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, with sampling laws $P_i$ and targets $q_i=q(x_i)$. Assume the metric-loss sections $a\mapsto d_Q(q_i,a)$ are $\mathcal G$-measurable. Let $\delta$ be one randomized decision rule from $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ to $(Q,\mathcal G)$, used under both specifications, and define its expected metric risk by
$$R_i(\delta)=\int_{\mathsf Y}\left(\int_Q d_Q(q_i,a)\,\delta(y,da)\right)P_i(dy).$$
If $P_0=P_1$ and $\Delta=d_Q(q_0,q_1)$, then
$$\max\{R_0(\delta),R_1(\delta)\}\ge\frac{\Delta}{2}.$$
Each risk is an extended nonnegative integral; deterministic measurable estimators are included as point-mass decision kernels. This theorem makes no assertion when the observation laws differ, and quantitative robustness requires a separately established stability modulus.
items.strategy: Integrate the pointwise metric triangle inequality under the common decision kernel and common observation law, then compare the sum of the two risks with their maximum.

references.title: Maxim Raginsky, Minimax lower bounds, §1, Lemma 1 and complete proof, PDF pp. 3–5
John Duchi, Lecture Notes on Statistics and Information Theory, Chapter 8, §§8.1–8.3

title: Unknown operators, model mismatch, and robustness limits — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A restricted two-operator class with a positive stability modulus
items.statement:
Let the truth space be $U=[1,2]\cup[4,5]$ with its absolute-value metric, the operator labels be $\mathfrak A=\{1,2\}$, and the data space be $\mathbb R$ with its absolute-value metric. For each label $a$, define $F_a(x)=ax$ on $U$. Restrict the admissible truth/operator pairs to
$$\mathcal C=\{(x,1):1\le x\le2\}\cup\{(x,2):4\le x\le5\}\subseteq U\times\mathfrak A,$$
with the restriction to $\mathcal C$ of the metric $d_1((x,a),(x',a'))=|x-x'|+|a-a'|$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Take $Q=q(\mathcal C)=U$ with its absolute-value metric and target map $q(x,a)=x$; the recovery equivalence on $\mathcal C$ is equality. The configuration forward map is $G(x,a)=F_a(x)=ax$. Then $\omega(t)=t$ is a uniform stability modulus: for every $c,c'\in\mathcal C$, $|q(c)-q(c')|\le\omega(|G(c)-G(c')|)$.
items.strategy: Verify the target-to-data distance inequality within each operator branch and across the two separated branches.

items.title: Distinct truths and operators with identical noisy data laws
items.statement:
Let the truth space and target space both be $\mathbb R$ with their absolute-value metric, and take the action sigma-algebra to be the power set $\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$, so every absolute metric-loss section is measurable. Let the admissible truth/operator pairs be $\mathbb R	imes\{A_0,A_1\}$ and take target map $q(x)=x$. Define the linear forward operators $A_0(x)=x$ and $A_1(x)=x/2$. Equip the data space $\mathbb R$ with its power-set sigma-algebra and usual addition, so every translation is measurable, and let $
u$ be any probability measure on that measurable space, for example the Dirac measure at $0$. The specifications $(1,A_0,
u)$ and $(2,A_1,
u)$ have the same data law, since both forward signals equal $1$, while their targets are distance $1$ apart. Every randomized decision rule into the stated action space therefore has maximum expected absolute loss at least $1/2$.
items.strategy: Compute the two forward signals, identify the translated noise laws, and apply the equal-law metric-risk theorem.
